To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
soil heterogeneity at small spatial scales facilitates the coexistence of competing earthworm species in the GF of the Colombian Llano.

1) species co-occured more frequently than expected, 2) the pattern was driven by the soil environmental heterogeneity and 3) species co-occur in a way that is compatible with coexistence aggregation model.

the coexistence aggregation hypothesis is supported in this study by showing that the spatial co-occurence of competing species is facilitated by soil heterogeneity at small spatial scales in a tropical GF of the Colombian Llano.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spatial distribution of species, the structure and composition of earthworm communities in a gallery forest and the relationship between earthworms and soil environmental heterogeneity.
the spatial structure of soil organisms at small scales, a topic that has been poorly studied in soil ecology.
the importance of spatial environmental heterogeneity in structuring the earthworm community in a gallery forest.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
soil environmental heterogeneity allows species co-occurrences in the studied GF.

the spatial aggregation of soil-feeding earthworms in the GF is facilitated by the spatial distribution of soil environmental heterogeneities and the spatial aggregation of litter-feeding species is facilitated by the distribution of litter resources and soil environmental heterogeneites.
the spatial distribution of soil environmental heterogeneities is an important factor for the co-occurrence pattern in this earthworm community.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatial aggregation model is a useful tool in soil ecology, and it should be used more often in studies on soil organisms.

the co-occurrence pattern observed for competing species was not the result of competition, but the result of spatial aggregation of competitors facilitated by soil environmental patchiness at small scales.
the soil environment is heterogeneous and this allows spatial co-occur- rence of competitor species at small spatial scales.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the coexistence of competitor earthworms in a GF was not random, and that spatial aggregation of species at small scales was facilitated by environmental heterogeneity.
spatial aggregation of soil organisms can be the consequence of the aggregation of resources, and not the other way around.
the study of species co-occurring patterns is relevant to understand the ecological processes structuring the earthworm community in the GF.
